name: Rosa Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in first-year law. A normal week is contract law lectures, a legal skills class where we practise reading statutes, and a Thursday seminar that always runs over. I have a room in a flat on Elm Gate with two other law students. I grew up in a small town, where my parents run a farm machinery dealership, and they pay for my fees and my rent. I go home most weekends if there's no deadline.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What kind of lawyer do you want to be?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A small-town one, the type who does wills, house sales and family matters, and knows everyone. Our family solicitor, Mr Brandt, is retiring, and nobody is replacing him. I want to go back and be that person. I use an AI tool occasionally to explain a statute, but I check it against the textbook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reassuring, but I'd keep quiet about it. I'd tell classmates that law is about people and judgement, and a chatbot doesn't change that. At home I'd say the same to my dad, who thinks the whole thing is nonsense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan holds: finish the degree, do the training, and go home to be the local solicitor. The only pressure is the cost of qualifying and my average results making it harder to get a training place. I'd need to be sensible and work hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and join the law society. I'd write to Mr Brandt and ask to shadow him for a week next summer. I'd use AI for summaries, because it does save time, but I'd keep checking the sources. And I'd save some of my allowance, since qualifying costs money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Life stays as it is, which is what I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting a training place with average marks. A lot of firms want top students, and I'm not one. I'd have to make up for it with experience and being willing to start in a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that mean for going home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have to work in the city for a few years first, then go back when I'm ready. Mum says that's fine, as long as I come back.

I'd tell my dad, who thinks the whole thing is **nonsense**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say law will change, but people will still need someone they trust. I'd tell friends that routine paperwork, searching and checking will go to software, and that the people side of the job matters more. I'd also say that small towns will need lawyers more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big firms and the junior jobs shrink, and that's where most training places are. That makes my average results a bigger problem. But a small-town practice depends on trust, and software can't be known by the family it has worked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at the tools, but carefully, using them for research and drafts. I'd look for work with small firms, since they hire for people and trust. I'd talk to Mr Brandt about taking over some of his clients. And I'd save more, because there may be a long wait for a training contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. There's a threat, but also a gap I could fill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad, who thinks it's nonsense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he's partly right, but even a dealership will use software for parts and orders. And I'd say I'll be fine, because someone has to be there when a farmer needs a will done properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about for the dealership?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordering and stock moving to software, and online competitors. The machines themselves are hands-on, so they'd be safer than my line of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that this is too fast and families need to stay together. I'd say we need our towns and churches to help people, because governments will be too slow. I'd tell my classmates to talk to their parents about money and plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Law is thinking work, and by 2028 I'd be in second year. By the time I qualify, there may be no training contracts. The dealership would last until about 2031, but farmers may lose their incomes too, if food prices or jobs change. It all feels linked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents about whether to keep going with the degree, and what the dealership could do for me. I'd stop spending money on things I don't need. I'd also ask Mr Brandt for advice on whether there's still a path for a small-town lawyer. I'd stay at home more on weekends and help with the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, a bit tearful. I'd phone my mum most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop studying law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I'd keep going while I work out a plan, because a degree is still something. But I'd stop assuming it leads to the job I wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan has no room to be slow. I'd have to decide things in months, not years. With a longer warning I could trust the plan to adjust itself.

I'd say towns and **churches** must help, because governments will be too slow.

fieldNote: Her **fear** is for her own path and her family's customers.
Falls back on **family** and church, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for the sensible people to get ready. I'd tell friends to look for what can't be done by machines, like looking after people, and being trusted. I'd say that families and towns should plan together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but I'd have a way through. By 2031 I'd be 23 and starting at a small firm or at Mr Brandt's practice. If he's retired, someone else needs to fill that gap. The risk is that the training places disappear before I get one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard for decent marks and get experience in small firms. I'd use AI a bit more, to be efficient. I'd save steadily, and I'd talk to my parents about whether they could lend me some money for the cost of qualifying. I'd also build contacts in my hometown, so people know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can cope with it. Five years is a decent amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently from the two-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calmer and I'd plan. In the two-year version I'd be reacting. Here I'd be building something, like trust in my home town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you build trust in a town before you qualify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Show up. Help at church events, do a legal advice evening with the law society, and let people see I'm serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people to adjust. I'd tell friends to get on with their lives and not change everything over a prediction. I'd say that small towns should look after their people and trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly calm. By 2036 I'd be 28, qualified, and back in my town. AI would handle a lot of the paperwork, and I'd be the person who explains things and makes decisions with families. I'd still worry about some people losing work, like the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, do the training, and go back home. I'd learn the tools as they come, with a bit of caution. I'd also help the dealership with any legal side, like contracts and staff matters, because that's a good way to start. And I'd save for a small office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long road and I'm on the right path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would AI change that small office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the paperwork and the searches. But the part where someone cries about a will, or argues about a boundary, isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for the people who lose work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Offer cheap advice evenings, and encourage the church and the council to set up training. I'd treat it as part of being the local lawyer.

I'd tell friends not to change everything over a **prediction**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 28, **qualified** and back in my town.
I'd still worry about people losing work, like **office** staff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years doesn't give me or my parents' customers time, and I'd be in the middle of my degree. What would help is honest advice from the law society and the government about training places, and help for small towns to keep their services.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to know small towns will still need people. Not everything is a city or a screen.

headlineQuote: Not everything is a city or a screen.
portrait: Rosa is an 18-year-old **law** student from a small town, where her parents run a farm machinery dealership and pay her fees.
She uses AI now and then, checks it against textbooks, and wants to return as the **solicitor** who replaces Mr Brandt.
She is traditional, trusts family, church and community over government, and plans to build **trust** in her hometown.
She is calm in the plateau, anxious in the middle worlds, and **alarmed** at two years, when training places could vanish.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world worries her most, because two years leaves no time for her or her parents' customers.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **advice** from the law society and government about training places, plus help for small towns to keep services.
